passage:
In the kasba panchayat office, Vikas the contractor held out a box of sweets. "Parul-ji, the whole block is talking about you. The youngest group leader, and the smartest. The women's hall will be your legacy. My team can start tomorrow."
Parul smiled and took one sweet. "Thank you, that's kind." She meant it; the words did feel good.
"So I'll bring the papers tonight?"
"Not tonight," she said. "We've asked for three quotes. The group will compare them on Saturday."
His smile thinned a little. On Saturday the women sat with the three papers. His quote was the most expensive and had no completion date. They chose a builder from the next village, and Parul sent Vikas a polite note thanking him for his interest.

qa.q: How many quotes did the group ask for?
qa.a: They asked for three quotes.

qa.q: How did Parul feel about Vikas's compliments?
qa.a: She was genuinely pleased and meant her thanks, since the words did feel good, but she didn't let them decide anything.

qa.q: What made Parul's response wise?
qa.a: She accepted the kind words, refused to rush, and let the group judge the quotes on price and completion date.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel when his smile thinned?
qa.a: He may have felt disappointed that his praise didn't speed things up, since he wanted the papers signed that night.

grounding: A young group leader enjoys a contractor's flattery but waits and judges his offer on its merits alongside other quotes.

passage:
Bao had run his tiny bakery in Melbourne for a year when Tomas, a flour supplier, walked in and tasted a pork bun.
"This is the best bun in the city," Tomas said. "I mean it. You're a real craftsman. A place like this deserves the best flour, and I'd love you to switch to us. Sign today, I'll throw in a discount."
Bao felt his chest swell. Nobody had said "craftsman" to him before.
"Thank you," he said, and meant it. "That's really kind."
Then he took the price sheet. "I'll look at this over the weekend and compare it with what I use now. I'll call you Monday."
"The discount's only for today," Tomas said.
"Then it'll have to be Monday's price," Bao said, smiling.
He enjoyed the compliment all evening. On Sunday he did the sums, tested a small bag, and decided the old flour was still better.

qa.q: When did Bao say he would call Tomas?
qa.a: He said he would call him Monday.

qa.q: How did Bao feel when Tomas called him a craftsman?
qa.a: Bao felt proud and touched, his chest swelling, because nobody had said that to him before.

qa.q: What did Bao do that kept praise separate from the decision?
qa.a: He thanked Tomas sincerely, refused the same-day pressure, and judged the flour on price and quality over the weekend.

qa.q: How might Tomas feel when Bao insists on waiting?
qa.a: Tomas might feel frustrated that his praise and today-only discount didn't secure a quick yes.

grounding: It shows an adult enjoying a supplier's praise, waiting before deciding, and judging the offer on its merits.

passage:
In the team lead's small glass cabin, Yusuf, the new joiner, sat down with a bright smile.
"Jeevan sir, I have to say, you're the best manager I've ever had. The way you run stand-ups is so calm. Everyone says so."
Jeevan smiled. "Thank you, Yusuf. That's kind of you to say."
"So I was wondering, since you know my work, could we skip the three-month probation review? It's just paperwork, right?"
Jeevan felt the warmth of the praise and the small tug that came with it. He paused, looking at his calendar before answering.
"I appreciate what you said, genuinely. But the review isn't paperwork. It's how we both see what's going well. Your onboarding tasks have been good, so you've nothing to worry about. Let's keep it on the 14th."
Yusuf nodded, slightly deflated. Jeevan wrote the date on his notepad and moved on to the next file.

qa.q: When is the probation review scheduled?
qa.a: On the 14th.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel when Yusuf asked to skip the review?
qa.a: Jeevan felt the warmth of the praise and a small tug to agree, which made him pause before answering.

qa.q: How did Jeevan keep the compliment separate from his decision?
qa.a: He thanked Yusuf genuinely, paused, and judged the request on its merits, keeping the review while reassuring him.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel after Jeevan's answer?
qa.a: Yusuf felt slightly deflated, since his praise did not change the decision.

grounding: It shows an adult accepting a kind word, pausing, and judging a request on its merits rather than being steered by flattery.

passage:
Subject: Re: your talk, and a proposal

Dear Divyansh,
Thank you for your lovely message about my talk at the teachers' conference. It genuinely made my week. I especially liked hearing that the story about my first class stayed with you.
You also asked whether I'd put my name on your new learning app as a "recommended by" expert, and join a launch video on Friday.
I've been flattered, and I've enjoyed that. But I'd like to keep the kind words and the decision separate. Before I can say yes, I'd need to see how the app works with real students, what data it collects from children, and who reviews its content.
Could you send me those details? I'll read them properly next week and let you know by the 20th. If it's a fit, I'll be glad to help. If Friday doesn't work for your timeline, I understand.
Warmly,
Nandini

qa.q: By what date does Nandini promise a reply?
qa.a: By the 20th.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel about Divyansh's message?
qa.a: Nandini felt genuinely pleased and grateful, saying it made the week, while staying careful about the request.

qa.q: What details does Nandini ask for before deciding?
qa.a: How the app works with real students, what data it collects from children, and who reviews its content.

qa.q: How might Divyansh see Nandini's reply?
qa.a: Divyansh might feel a little disappointed about Friday, but also respect that Nandini takes a public endorsement seriously.

grounding: An adult thanks someone warmly for praise while waiting to judge the request on its merits, keeping praise and decision separate.

passage: People ask me how you say no to someone who's being so nice. Honestly, I don't always. But here's what happened in spring. My cousin Jatin came to the shop and said the most beautiful things: that my blouses were the best stitching in Nagpur, that I had an eye no one else had. I felt ten feet tall. I said, "Thank you, Jatin, that means a lot," and I meant it. Then he asked if my two tailors could work at his wedding-season stall for three weekends. My instinct was to say yes on the spot, because no felt like throwing his kindness back at him. Instead I said, "Let me look at my orders and call you Thursday." On Thursday the orders said no. So I told him no, warmly. He sulked a bit, but we're fine. I'm Kalyani, and that's my trick: enjoy the praise tonight, decide the favour tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Jatin ask of Kalyani's tailors?
qa.a: He asked if the two tailors could work at his wedding-season stall for three weekends.

qa.q: Why was Kalyani tempted to say yes on the spot?
qa.a: Kalyani felt proud and touched by the praise, and refusing felt like throwing Jatin's kindness back at him.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who gets lavish praise followed by a favour?
qa.a: Thank the person sincerely, then set a time to decide, as Kalyani did by checking the orders before calling back on Thursday.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel when the answer is no?
qa.a: Jatin may feel disappointed and a bit sulky, but because the no came warmly and after real checking, the relationship stayed fine.

grounding: Shows a person who enjoys a kind word, waits before deciding, and judges the favour on its merits.
